hints: Look closely at the conditions, hot and ethanolic are the big clues here, not just sodium hydroxide.
Remember that aqueous NaOH gives substitution to an alcohol, while hot ethanolic NaOH makes OH- act as a base for elimination.
If you remove HBr from $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$, think about what C=C containing hydrocarbon must be left.
walkthrough:
**Spot the reaction conditions**

Great start, always read the conditions first. Aqueous NaOH means substitution, but hot ethanolic NaOH means elimination.

Condition rule:
$$\text{hot ethanolic NaOH} \rightarrow \text{elimination, dehydrohalogenation}$$

**Apply elimination to 2-bromopropane**

Here OH- acts as a base, not a nucleophile. It removes a H+ from a carbon next to the C-Br, the C-Br bond breaks, and a C=C double bond forms.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3 + \text{NaOH} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\text{ethanol}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Identify the major product**

The product has three carbons with one double bond and no bromine or oxygen. That is the alkene propene, so elimination wins over substitution here.

options.A: Incorrect. Propan-1-ol is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, a primary alcohol. Substitution at C-2 could never move the OH to C-1 without rearrangement, and substitution does not happen in hot ethanolic conditions anyway.
options.B: Incorrect. Propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, is the substitution product. You would get this with hot aqueous NaOH where OH- acts as a nucleophile, not with hot ethanolic NaOH where it acts as a base.
options.C: Incorrect. 2-hydroxypropene would try to combine both an alkene and an alcohol, which does not form here. Enols like this are also very unstable and this option is a distractor mixing up elimination and substitution.
options.D: Correct. Hot ethanolic NaOH causes dehydrohalogenation (elimination of HBr) from 2-bromopropane. Loss of H from C-1 and Br from C-2 gives the C=C double bond in propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$.
